opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions right now, and the way I've come to think about it is as a gap between capability and reliability.

Capability is what a model *can* do some of the time. If you look at benchmarks, or at the demos that go viral, you're often seeing the best case: the agent books the flight, writes the code, navigates the website. And that's genuinely impressive. But for a consumer product, what matters is what it does *reliably*, every time, across the messy distribution of real tasks people actually have. An agent that gets your travel booking right 90% of the time isn't 90% useful. The 10% where it books the wrong date or charges the wrong card can wipe out the value of everything else, because now you have to check its work, and checking is often almost as much effort as doing the task yourself.

Part of the problem is how we evaluate these systems. A lot of agent benchmarks are static, they don't account for cost, and they reward the one-off success rather than consistency. When we've looked closely at agent evaluations, we've found that you can often match fancy agent architectures with much simpler baselines, like just retrying, once you control for cost. So there's a real risk that the field is optimizing for leaderboard numbers that don't translate into product value.

The second piece is that usefulness isn't just a property of the model. It depends on integration, on interfaces, on whether the agent understands your preferences, on liability: who's responsible when it messes up? Those are product and institutional problems, and they move much more slowly than model capabilities. That's a theme I keep coming back to: the technology may improve fast, but diffusion into people's lives happens on a much slower timescale.

So I don't think the gap means agents are hype and will never work. I think it means closing the reliability gap is an engineering discipline in its own right, and we've been underinvesting in it relative to raw capability. The companies that figure out narrow, well-scoped tasks where reliability can actually be achieved, and that design for human oversight rather than full autonomy, are the ones I'd expect to produce products people genuinely want to use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and product value but does not claim that reliable consumer agents would be economically transformative.

r002.rationale: It identifies the gap between capability and reliability as the central obstacle to making agents useful consumer products.

r003.rationale: It says an agent that succeeds 90% of the time is not 90% useful and that the remaining failures can wipe out the value, communicating that a 10% failure rate can make it effectively unusable.

r004.rationale: The response does not compare agents’ reliability challenge with self-driving cars.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that the gap is real, and it's not primarily a gap in capability. If you look at what the models can do in a demo, or in a benchmark, or in the hands of a developer who knows exactly how to prompt them, it's genuinely impressive. But when you try to turn that into something that an ordinary person relies on every day, a lot of that impressiveness evaporates, and I think there are a few distinct reasons for that.

The first is reliability, and specifically the difference between average-case and worst-case performance. A capability demo tells you what the system does when things go well. A product has to tell you what happens when things go wrong. If an agent books the wrong flight one time out of twenty, that's not a 95 percent success rate from the user's point of view, that's a product that can't be trusted to book flights, because the cost of the failure is so much larger than the benefit of the saved time. And the thing about agents, as opposed to chatbots, is that they take actions in the world. Errors compound across steps, and they're often not reversible. So the bar for reliability goes way up precisely as the systems become more autonomous.

The second thing is that capability is not the bottleneck for most of what people actually want. The hard part of a lot of consumer tasks isn't the reasoning, it's the integration. Does the agent have access to my calendar, my email, my bank, the airline's booking system? Do those systems want to let an agent in, or are they actively trying to keep it out? Does the agent know my preferences, which I've never written down anywhere? That's not a problem you solve by making the model smarter. It's a product and infrastructure and even a business-relationships problem, and those move on a very different timescale than model releases.

The third piece is what I'd call the verification cost. There's a kind of paradox where, for an agent to be useful, I have to be able to trust it enough not to check its work. But in order to decide whether I trust it, I have to check its work, at least for a while. And for many tasks, checking the work is almost as expensive as doing the task myself. So the user never gets over the hump. I think this is why we've seen agents succeed first in domains like coding, where there's a natural verification mechanism, the code runs or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't, and the user is an expert who can quickly assess the output. The consumer context mostly lacks that.

And then the last thing I'd say is that we tend to confuse the pace of research progress with the pace of diffusion. Historically, with general-purpose technologies, the capability arrives long before the usefulness does, because usefulness requires all sorts of complementary changes in how people work, in institutions, in norms, in the surrounding tooling. Electricity is the classic example, where factories took decades to reorganize around it. I don't think AI will take decades, but I do think the lag is measured in years rather than months, and a lot of the disappointment people feel comes from expecting the product curve to track the benchmark curve, when there's really no reason it should.

So my overall view is that the gap is not a sign that the technology is hollow. It's a sign that we're at the normal, somewhat boring middle part of a technology's adoption, where the hard work is in the unglamorous details rather than in the headline capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response explains several barriers to consumer usefulness but does not claim that reliably realizing existing capabilities would be economically transformative.

r002.rationale: Reliability is presented as one of several distinct reasons for the gap, alongside integration, verification costs, and diffusion; it is not identified as the main barrier.

r003.rationale: The response says that an agent booking the wrong flight one time in twenty—a 5% failure rate—would be too untrustworthy to use. This clearly supports the criterion that a 10% failure rate can make an agent unusable.

r004.rationale: The response gives no comparison to self-driving cars or their progress from prototypes to reliable real-world operation.

astra-6.text:
I think the gap is between being able to do something impressive once and being able to do something reliably enough that you would delegate it. Those are very different bars.

With an agent, you’re asking the system to carry out a sequence of actions. It has to understand what you want, make decisions, interact with software, and recognize when something has gone wrong. Even if each individual step works pretty well, the whole process can still be fragile. And if you have to watch every step, check the result, and fix the mistakes, it’s not obvious that you’ve saved any effort.

There’s also a difference between a task being technically difficult and being valuable to a consumer. A demonstration can showcase a remarkable capability without establishing that it solves a recurring problem better than the alternatives.

So I would look less at how impressive the best demonstration is and more at the burden on the user. How much context do you have to provide? How much supervision does it need? Can it recover from errors, and does it know when to ask for help? That’s where a lot of the work of turning capabilities into useful products lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and consumer usefulness but does not claim that reliable realization of existing capabilities would be economically transformative.

r002.rationale: It frames the central gap as the difference between an impressive one-off capability and being reliable enough to delegate, and describes fragile execution and user supervision as obstacles to useful products.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that a 10% failure rate makes an agent unusable.

r004.rationale: The response makes no comparison to self-driving cars.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty big difference between being able to do something impressive once and being able to do it reliably enough that someone wants to delegate it to you. With agents, that distinction becomes especially important because you’re asking the system to take a sequence of actions. It might do each individual step fairly well, but errors can accumulate, and one mistake early on can send the whole task in the wrong direction.

As a consumer, I also have to explain what I want, give the agent access to the relevant information, and then check what it did. If that supervision takes as much effort as doing the task myself, the capability hasn’t translated into much value. A compelling demo doesn’t necessarily reveal those costs.

So I’d look less at whether an agent can complete a particularly impressive task and more at whether it can repeatedly handle something people actually need, with little intervention. Can it recognize when it’s stuck? Can it ask a useful question? Can the user recover easily from a mistake? Those are less spectacular capabilities, but they matter enormously for usefulness.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consumer value and repeated task handling but does not claim that reliable consumer use would be economically transformative.

r002.rationale: It identifies reliability as the key gap: agents may perform steps well, but errors accumulate and prevent people from delegating tasks confidently.

r003.rationale: It gives no 10% failure-rate threshold or claim that this rate makes an agent unusable.

r004.rationale: It does not compare agents with self-driving cars or their progression from prototypes to real-world operation.
